name: Beth Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a crew for Southfield Energy, out of the Brook Lane depot in Ashby. Ashby's growing like mad, new housing estates everywhere, so a lot of my week is connecting new streets: running cable from the main line, setting the green boxes on the pavement, hooking up the meters. The rest is fixing what breaks. I like seeing a field turn into a street with lights on. What wears me out is the developers changing their minds and the mud, always the mud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come into the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Late, at twenty-eight. I was cleaning offices at night and saw an advert for an apprenticeship that took women. My dad thought I'd last a month. That was thirty years ago this spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use it now and then, it's handy, but I never thought it'd change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper and that's about it. My mate Joanne at the depot showed me how to get it to explain the new safety rules in plain words, and that saves me an evening. I'd say that, then go back to whatever we were talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be happy enough. I'm at the point where I want things to stay put until I retire at sixty-three. Rob drives a delivery van, and I'd be relieved for him too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Use it for the odd email or rule change. Keep our savings where they are, about four months, and keep paying the extra on the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use it for, beyond safety rules?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a developer sent us a contract that was twelve pages of nonsense, and I asked it what we'd actually agreed to. It told me in five lines. I still had my supervisor read it, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you be relieved for Rob?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he's been hearing about driverless vans for years. If this is all AI does, he can keep driving his route till he's done. He likes his route, he knows every dog on it.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful helper and that's about it. It explains new safety rules in plain words and saves me an evening.
S0.think: I'd be happy enough, because I want things to stay put until I retire at sixty-three. I'd be relieved for my husband, who drives a delivery van.
S0.do: Keeps working as she is, using AI now and then for emails and rule changes. Keeps about four months of savings and keeps paying extra on the car loan.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved for her husband.
S0.quote: He likes his route, he knows every dog on it.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is a practical, occasional AI user who checks its work with a person. Her first thought in a safe picture is relief for her husband's driving job. She came into the trade late and seems proud of having proved people wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's probably closer to real life, I'd think. And it's Rob's job I'd be thinking about, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen, so let's be sensible and train people up. Companies and government both have to do their bit, and workers do too. I'm not one for shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job's fine for a good while, people still need a cable dug in. But Rob's van could be driving itself in a few years, and he's sixty. That's our household cut in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting an extra hundred and fifty a month into savings from now. I'd use the new tools at work once the others are, I'm no first adopter. And I'd sit with Rob and look at what else he could do, maybe the warehouse side, or a forklift licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Rob say when you've talked about driverless vans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says they'll never manage the estate behind the school, where the cars park on both sides. I hope he's right. But they said that about a lot of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to find that hundred and fifty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The streaming services, we've got four and watch one. Takeaway on Fridays. And I'd stop sending Liam money for his phone, he's twenty-six.

S1.say: I'd say it's going to happen, so let's be sensible and train people up. Companies, government and workers all have to do their bit.
S1.think: My job is fine for a good while, but my husband's delivery van could drive itself in a few years. That would cut our household income in half.
S1.do: Puts an extra hundred and fifty a month into savings by cutting streaming, Friday takeaways and money for her son's phone. Uses new tools at work once colleagues do and helps her husband look at warehouse or forklift work.
S1.feel: Uneasy about the household rather than herself.
S1.quote: I'd stop sending Liam money for his phone, he's twenty-six.
S1.fieldNote: Beth's worry lives in her husband's job, not hers, which makes this picture more serious for her household than for her trade. She spreads responsibility evenly between companies, government and workers. Her savings plan is precise down to cancelled streaming services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, with robots. So both of us. Me and Rob. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to put something in place quickly, a bridge for people until they find their feet. I'm not usually one for big state schemes, but two years is no time. I'd say that at the depot and to friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. Rob's van would go first, then maybe the cable work if they've got robots that can dig and joint. Four months of savings with both of us out, and I'd be three years short of my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all extra spending straight away, no holiday, no new kitchen tiles. Within a few months we'd look at selling the house and buying something smaller, maybe in Rob's home town, Kirby, where it's cheaper. I'd apply for whatever support the government put out, and I'd ask the company about early retirement terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about selling the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emma would cry, she grew up in that house. Liam would say "where's my room going to be", like he's not twenty-six. I'd tell them we're not going under, we're just getting smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not one for big state schemes, but you'd apply. Does that feel uncomfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I've paid in for thirty years, and if the whole country's hit at once, that's what it's for. I wouldn't be proud about it, I'd just do it.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to put a bridge in place quickly for people until they find their feet. I'm not usually for big state schemes, but two years is no time.
S2.think: I'd be scared, because my husband's van would go first and then maybe my cable work. Four months of savings with both of us out, and three years short of my pension.
S2.do: Stops all extra spending at once and within months looks at selling the house to buy something smaller in a cheaper town. Applies for any government support and asks the company about early retirement terms.
S2.quote: I'd tell them we're not going under, we're just getting smaller.
S2.fieldNote: This picture hits two incomes in one house, which pushes Beth to alarm. She is open about the tension between her usual dislike of state schemes and her willingness to use them in a crisis. Downsizing is her concrete escape route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That changes it. That's time to get things in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if people start now. Retraining for people like Rob, pensions sorted for people like me. I'd say it calmly, it's not the end of the world with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd make it to sixty-three just as it lands, give or take. Like I said with the fast one, it's Rob I worry about, his van would probably go well before 2031. But five years gives him time to move to something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push savings up to two hundred a month. I'd get Rob onto a course this year, the college in Ashby does forklift and warehouse management. I'd also pick up more of the new tools at work once the crew starts using them, so I'm not the one left behind in my last two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a manageable kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would warehouse work be safe for Rob, if robots come by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for long, no. But it might get him to sixty-five, and that's all he needs. We're not planning for forty years, just for a few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still sell the house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, after I retire, on our terms. Not in a panic. That's the difference five years makes.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if people start now, with retraining for people like my husband and sorted pensions for people like me. It's not the end of the world.
S3.think: I'd reach sixty-three just as it lands, give or take. My husband's van would probably go well before 2031, but five years gives him time to move.
S3.do: Raises savings to two hundred a month and gets her husband onto a forklift and warehouse course this year. Picks up new work tools as the crew adopts them and plans to downsize later, on their own terms.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way she feels she can manage.
S3.quote: We're not planning for forty years, just for a few.
S3.fieldNote: Beth sees clearly that she and her husband only need to bridge a few years, not a career. Five years turns the panic sale of the house into a choice made later. She'd keep up with tools at work so as not to be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'll be retired, and Rob too, if all goes well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years, everyone should be planning. I'd tell the young ones on the crew to keep learning and not get stuck. I wouldn't make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, for Rob and me it's mostly fine, we'd both be retired before it lands. I'd worry about Liam, he works in a warehouse, and that's exactly what robots will do. Emma's a teacher, I think she's safer, but I don't really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and retire at sixty-three. Keep the extra savings going, about a hundred and fifty. And I'd nag Liam to get some kind of qualification, he's been drifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Liam. Calm about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of qualification would you nag him about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd tell him to come and do my trade. He'd laugh. But robots or not, the estates keep getting built, and I'd rather he learned something with his hands than sat waiting for a warehouse to close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Emma is safer but you don't really know. What makes you unsure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says they're already using AI to mark homework. If it can mark it, maybe it can teach it, I don't know. She'd tell me kids need a person, and I'd believe her.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years and everyone should be planning. I'd tell the young ones on the crew to keep learning.
S4.think: For my husband and me it's mostly fine because we'd both be retired before it lands. I'd worry about my son, who works in a warehouse.
S4.do: Carries on working and retires at sixty-three as planned, keeping extra savings of about a hundred and fifty a month. Pushes her son to get a qualification, perhaps in her own trade.
S4.feel: Calm about herself and her husband, uneasy for her son.
S4.quote: I'd rather he learned something with his hands than sat waiting for a warehouse to close.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years takes Beth and her husband out of the firing line, so her worry moves to her drifting son. She is honest about not knowing whether her daughter's teaching job is safe. She keeps her calm, sensible tone throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes Rob's job and maybe mine at the same time, and that's the house gone. What would help is a bridge, some income for a couple of years for people near retirement, and the company letting us go early without losing the pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the estates. Somebody's still going to live in those houses we connect, and they'll want power on Christmas Day. I'd like to know who's going to answer that call, a robot or a person.

headlineQuote: Somebody's still going to live in those houses we connect, and they'll want power on Christmas Day.
portrait: Beth Fischer is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker for Southfield Energy in fast-growing Ashby, where she connects new housing estates to the grid; she came into the trade at twenty-eight after cleaning offices. She uses AI now and then and takes up new tools once colleagues have. Her main worry across the pictures is her husband Rob's delivery driving job, which makes even the slow-change picture a household concern. AGI by 2028 alarms her because both their incomes could go at once, and she would sell the house and accept government help. With five or ten years she plans calmly, retraining Rob and nagging her son towards a trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it could take her husband's job and hers at the same time and cost them the house.
whatWouldHelp: A bridging income for a couple of years for people near retirement, and early retirement from the company without losing her pension.
